claim: Activating BRAF mutations (e.g. BRAFV600E) are the most common oncogenic mutations in melanoma, seen in about 66% of cases.
source: Activating BRAF mutations (e.g. BRAFV600E) are the most common oncogenic mutations in melanoma, seen in about 66% of cases (Davies et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davies et al., 2002

claim: The BRAFV600E mutation is found in 89% of melanocytic nevi.
source: Curiously, the same mutation is found in 89% of melanocytic nevi (Pollock et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pollock et al., 2003

claim: Melanocyte-specific expression of BRAFV600E efficiently produces nevi, but only very rarely melanoma in animal studies.
source: In animal studies, melanocyte-specific expression of BRAFV600E efficiently produces nevi, but only very rarely melanoma (Dankort et al., 2009; Dhomen et al., 2009; Patton et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple animal studies

claim: The widely-accepted explanation for nevus growth arrest is that transformed melanocytes undergo oncogene-induced senescence (OIS).
source: The widely-accepted explanation is that transformed melanocytes undergo oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), arresting proliferation before additional oncogenic events can occur (e.g. Bennett, 2003; Huang et al., 2017; Kaplon et al., 2014; Michaloglou et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature

claim: Nevus melanocytes are growth-arrested.
source: Nevus melanocytes are indeed growth-arrested, but the assumption that OIS is the cause remains untested, in part because of a lack of criteria to rigorously define OIS in vivo (Damsky and Bosenberg, 2017).
evidence: Stated as established fact with citation

claim: No single hallmark distinguishes senescence from other growth-arrested cell states.
source: Yet no single hallmark distinguishes senescence from other growth-arrested cell states.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about senescence markers

claim: Phenotypes once thought to be 'gold standards' for senescence, such as expression of lysosomal beta-galactosidase, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, or p53, commonly mark only subsets of senescent cells.
source: Phenotypes once thought to be 'gold standards', such as expression of lysosomal beta-galactosidase, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, or p53, commonly mark only subsets of senescent cells (Wiley et al., 2017), as well as non-senescent cells (Tran et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wiley et al., 2017 and Tran et al., 2012

claim: Observations of supposedly senescent cells resuming proliferation imply that permanent cell cycle exit cannot be used as a distinguishing feature of senescence.
source: Moreover, observations of supposedly senescent cells resuming proliferation (e.g. Beauséjour et al., 2003), imply that permanent cell cycle exit cannot be used as a distinguishing feature.
evidence: Inference based on cited observations

claim: In mice whose back skin was treated with topical 4-OHT at postnatal day 2 (P2), P3 and P4, nevi were apparent macroscopically at telogen (P50).
source: As shown in Figure 1, in mice whose back skin was treated with topical 4-OHT at postnatal day 2 (P2), P3 and P4, nevi were apparent macroscopically at telogen (P50; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Mouse nevi consist of scattered nests of pigment-containing cells, like human nevi.
source: Live imaging, using multi-photon microscopy (MPM; Saager et al., 2015), revealed that, like human nevi, mouse nevi consist of scattered nests of pigment-containing cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 1B

claim: When forepaws were treated with 4-OHT from P2 through P4, tiny nevi could be detected as early as P6.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, when forepaws were treated with 4-OHT from P2 through P4, tiny nevi could be detected as early as P6.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1D

claim: Most nevi reach a maximum size somewhere between P16 and P21.
source: Serial observation indicated that most nevi reach a maximum size somewhere between P16 and P21 (Figure 1D , Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by serial observation data shown in figures

claim: In the mouse, BrafV600E-transformed melanocytes arrest within 2–3 weeks.
source: This suggests that, in the mouse, BrafV600E-transformed melanocytes arrest within 2–3 weeks.
evidence: Inference from the observation that nevi reach maximum size between P16 and P21

claim: By P21, nests within nevi were uniformly negative for BrdU, implying growth arrest.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, albino mice generate nests similar to those seen in pigmented mice. In such animals, BrdU readily incorporated into hair follicle melanocytes (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), whereas by p21 nests within nevi were uniformly negative for BrdU, implying growth arrest (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling data shown in figures

claim: Braf-induced nevi are already growth-arrested by P21.
source: The conclusion that Braf-induced nevi are already growth-arrested by P21 agrees with the reports of others (Damsky and Bosenberg, 2017)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation

claim: Nest size distributions change insignificantly between P21 and P50.
source: and is lent further support by time course measurements of nest size by MPM (Figure 1C), which show that nest size distributions change insignificantly between P21 and P50 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Supported by time course measurements shown in figures

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing identified 14 different cell types in the skin, including melanocytes.
source: Using known cell-type marker genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B), we identified 14 different cell types in the skin, including melanocytes (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in figures

claim: Unsupervised clustering sub-divided the melanocytes into four groups.
source: Unsupervised clustering further sub-divided the melanocytes into four groups (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mel 0 and Mel 1 melanocyte clusters were composed of cells found only in nevus-bearing, and not wildtype, skin.
source: Two of them, Mel 0 and Mel 1, were composed of cells found only in nevus-bearing, and not wildtype, skin (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Mel 0 and Mel 1 are identified as the 'nevus melanocytes', because they are seen only when nevi are present, and are by far the predominant melanocyte population in such animals.
source: We identify them as the 'nevus melanocytes', because they are seen only when nevi are present, and are by far the predominant melanocyte population in such animals.
evidence: Inference from the observation that these clusters are only found in nevus-bearing animals

claim: Mel 0 and Mel 1 are highly similar in gene expression, primarily differing in having a slightly lower level of pigment gene expression in Mel 1 versus Mel 0.
source: they are highly similar in gene expression, primarily differing in having a slightly lower level of pigment gene expression in Mel 1 versus Mel 0 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Mel 2 cells express the lowest levels of pigmentation genes and are seen in both genotypes at all stages.
source: Mel 2 cells express the lowest levels of pigmentation genes (Figure 2D), and are seen in both genotypes (Figure 2C) at all stages (although expanded in number in nevus-bearing animals (Figure 2F)).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and clustering data shown in figures

claim: Mel 2 cells' pattern of gene expression bears a strong resemblance to one recently published for melanocyte stem cells isolated from telogen-stage hair follicles.
source: Their pattern of gene expression bears a strong resemblance to one recently published for melanocyte stem cells isolated from telogen-stage hair follicles (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison with published data from Zhang et al., 2020

claim: Mel 2 cells express Cd34, which has been proposed to be a marker for bulge-associated melanocyte stem cells.
source: In particular, they express Cd34, which has been proposed to be a marker for bulge-associated melanocyte stem cells (Joshi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data and citation to Joshi et al., 2019

claim: Cells of cluster Mel 3 express the highest levels of pigment genes and are found in both mutant and wildtype mice, but only at the P30 time point.
source: Finally, cells of cluster Mel 3, which express the highest levels of pigment genes (Figure 2D), are found in both mutant and wildtype mice, but only at the P30 time point (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and temporal analysis shown in figures

claim: Mel 3 cells are identified as mature hair follicle melanocytes, as such cells are present exclusively during anagen phase of the hair cycle (P30), and disappear during telogen (P50).
source: We thus identify them as mature hair follicle melanocytes, as such cells are present exclusively during anagen phase of the hair cycle (P30), and disappear during telogen (P50).
evidence: Inference from temporal expression patterns and knowledge of hair cycle biology

claim: Patterns of gene expression in arrested nevus melanocytes fail to identify them as any more senescent than other skin cells or normal melanocytes.
source: First, patterns of gene expression in arrested nevus melanocytes fail to identify them as any more senescent than other skin cells or normal melanocytes, arguing against a primary role for any form of senescence in their arrest.
evidence: Supported by gene expression signature analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: The timing and statistics of nevus formation effectively argue against any relatively simple cell-autonomous process as being the cause of growth arrest.
source: Second, the timing and statistics of nevus formation effectively argue against any relatively simple cell-autonomous process as being the cause of growth arrest.
evidence: Supported by modeling and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Using the 'Classical' signature, only Cdkn2a stands out as strongly upregulated in nevus melanocytes, but it is similarly upregulated in skin fibroblasts.
source: When compared with whole skin, using the 'Classical' signature, only Cdkn2a stands out as strongly upregulated in nevus melanocytes, but it is similarly upregulated in skin fibroblasts (it also has the noisiest data among genes in the signature).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: With the 'Universal Up' signature, more genes are downregulated than upregulated in nevus melanocytes.
source: With the 'Universal Up' signature, more genes are downregulated than upregulated in nevus melanocytes.
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Skin fibroblasts better fit the 'Classical' senescent signature than any skin cell type, including nevus melanocytes, or indeed melanocytes of any cluster.
source: The results suggest that skin fibroblasts better fit the 'Classical' senescent signature than any skin cell type, including nevus melanocytes, or indeed melanocytes of any cluster.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of gene expression signatures shown in Figure 3B

claim: The meta-PCNA signature identified two keratinocyte populations ('IFE-cycling' and 'Outer Bulge 1') as highly proliferative.
source: As shown in Figure 3B (also see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), this signature (122 genes of which had unambiguous mouse orthologs; Source data 1) identified two keratinocyte populations ('IFE-cycling' and 'Outer Bulge 1') as highly proliferative (in agreement with Joost et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by gene expression signature analysis shown in figures

claim: The meta-PCNA signature correctly identified nevus melanocytes as non-proliferative and other melanocytes as proliferative.
source: Importantly, it also correctly identified nevus melanocytes as non-proliferative—and other melanocytes as proliferative—in agreement with Figure 1E–F.
evidence: Supported by gene expression signature analysis consistent with BrdU labeling data

claim: The relatively high expression of proliferation-associated genes in non-nevus, hair follicle melanocytes (Mel 3) when compared with nevus melanocytes, was consistent between BrafV600E-expressing and control mice.
source: Interestingly, the relatively high expression of proliferation-associated genes in non-nevus, hair follicle melanocytes (Mel 3) when compared with nevus melanocytes, was consistent between BrafV600E-expressing and control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by gene expression comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Tissue context plays a role in whether BrafV600E-expressing cells even arrest growth.
source: suggesting that tissue context plays a role in whether BrafV600E-expressing cells even arrest growth.
evidence: Inference from the observation that proliferation gene expression differs between nevus and hair follicle melanocytes regardless of Braf status

claim: In five of eight senescence signature cases, nevus melanocytes rank as less senescent than the average skin cell.
source: In five of the eight cases, nevus melanocytes rank as less senescent than the average skin cell; in two of the cases nevus melanocytes are about average.
evidence: Supported by analysis of multiple senescence signatures shown in Figure 3C and supplements

claim: In only one case ('Chatsirisupachai Down') does nevus melanocyte gene expression go in the predicted direction for senescence.
source: In only one case ('Chatsirisupachai Down') does nevus melanocyte gene expression go in the predicted direction for senescence.
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: The Chatsirisupachai Down signature is more likely a signature of proliferation than 'non-senescence'.
source: However, the Chatsirisupachai signatures had not been curated to remove genes associated simply with proliferation/quiescence (Chatsirisupachai et al., 2019), and inspection of the 'Chatsirisupachai Down' gene list shows that 61 of its 250 genes are shared with the 129-gene meta-PCNA signature; that is it is more likely a signature of proliferation than 'non-senescence'
evidence: Inference from overlap analysis between gene signatures

claim: Of the 23 'Universal Down' signature genes in BRAFV600E-transduced human melanocytes, 15 were significantly differentially expressed, and 100% of these were decreased in expression.
source: Of the 23 'Universal Down' signature genes, 15 were significantly differentially expressed, and 100% of these were decreased in expression.
evidence: Analysis of published data from Pawlikowski et al., 2013 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Of the 31 'Universal Up' genes in BRAFV600E-transduced human melanocytes, 19 were significantly differentially expressed, and 84% of these were elevated in expression.
source: Of the 31 'Universal Up' genes, 19 were significantly differentially expressed, and 84% of these were elevated in expression.
evidence: Analysis of published data from Pawlikowski et al., 2013 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The data do not support the view that any sort of senescence—oncogene-induced or otherwise—is characteristic of nevus melanocytes and therefore a possible cause of their growth arrest.
source: Together these data do not support the view that any sort of senescence—oncogene-induced or otherwise—is characteristic of nevus melanocytes and therefore a possible cause of their growth arrest.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comprehensive gene expression signature analysis

claim: If the per-cell-cycle senescence probability (s) is less than 0.5, then some clones will never stop growing.
source: If s < 0.5, (i.e. less than a 50% chance of arrest per cell cycle), then some clones will never stop growing.
evidence: Mathematical result from stochastic modeling

claim: To achieve 99% clonal arrest by 30 cell cycles, s must be around 0.56 or higher; to achieve arrest in 95% of clones, s must be greater than 0.52.
source: To achieve 99% clonal arrest by 30 cell cycles, s must be around 0.56 or higher; to achieve arrest in 95% of clones, s must be greater than 0.52 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Results from Monte Carlo simulations shown in Figure 4A

claim: A value of s that enables 95% of clones to arrest produces a mean clone size of only 18.5 cells.
source: For example, a value of s that enables 95% of clones to arrest produces a mean clone size of only 18.5 cells.
evidence: Results from simulations shown in Figure 4B

claim: Cell numbers per nevus are estimated to be in the range of 100–1000 cells.
source: For comparison, we estimate cell numbers per nevus to be in the range of 100–1000 cells (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Estimation based on measurements described in Materials and methods

claim: Simulated clone size distributions are extremely heavy-tailed, with a very large number of very small clones and a small number of very large clones.
source: As shown in Figure 4C–D, such distributions are extremely heavy-tailed, with a very large number of very small clones and a small number of very large clones
evidence: Results from simulations shown in Figure 4C-D

claim: Nevi displayed a mean radius of 76.8 µm (corresponding to an area of 0.019 mm2).
source: Nevi displayed a mean radius of 76.8 µm (corresponding to an area of 0.019 mm2, in excellent agreement with the results of Damsky et al., 2015)
evidence: Measurement from experimental data, consistent with published results

claim: When plotted on a logarithmic scale, individual nevus radii displayed a Gaussian-like distribution (log-normal).
source: and, when plotted on a logarithmic scale, individual radii displayed a Gaussian-like distribution (Figure 4E; a Gaussian shape on a logarithmic axis is usually referred to as 'log-normal').
evidence: Observation from data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Nest sizes are log-normally distributed whether at P21 or P50.
source: Interestingly, nest sizes (quantified by MPM) also seem to be log-normally distributed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) whether at P21 (panel A) or P50 (panel B).
evidence: Observation from data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The nests within human melanocytic nevi are log-normally distributed, despite being an order of magnitude larger than those in mice.
source: So are the nests within human melanocytic nevi, despite the latter being an order of magnitude larger than those in mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Observation from human nevus data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: The relative shapes of simulated distributions were about the same regardless of where they were truncated.
source: As it turns out, the relative shapes of simulated distributions were about the same regardless of where they were truncated.
evidence: Result from simulation analysis

claim: For s reasonably close to 0.5, the approximate probability of observing any clone size can be shown analytically to vary inversely with the 3/2-power of size.
source: In fact, for s reasonably close to 0.5, the approximate probability of observing any clone size can be shown analytically to vary inversely with the 3/2-power of size (for derivation, see Appendix 1).
evidence: Mathematical derivation provided in Appendix 1

claim: Observed nevus size distributions cannot be generated by any cell-autonomous, random, time independent, one-step process.
source: These data imply that observed nevus size distributions cannot be generated by any cell-autonomous, random, time independent, one-step process.
evidence: Conclusion from comparison of simulations with empirical data

claim: To achieve clonal stopping times within 30 cell cycles, the minimum per-step transition probability increases with the number of steps.
source: First, to achieve clonal stopping times within 30 cell cycles, the minimum per-step transition probability increases with the number of steps (Figure 4F).
evidence: Results from multi-step simulations shown in Figure 4F

claim: If it takes three random events to arrest growth in 99% of clones, the average probability of each event needs to be at least 0.66 per cell cycle.
source: For example, if it takes three random events to arrest growth in 99% of clones, the average probability of each event needs to be at least 0.66 per cell cycle; with five random events that number is 0.74.
evidence: Results from multi-step simulations

claim: Distributions generated by multi-step models become less heavy-tailed as the number of steps increases, gradually approaching something that looks log-normal.
source: Second, although distributions generated by such models still tend to be heavy-tailed (Figure 4G), they become less so as the number of steps increases (Figure 4H), gradually approaching something that looks log-normal.
evidence: Results from multi-step simulations shown in Figure 4G-H

claim: To produce nevi of even 200 cells requires 4–5 independent events (stages), depending on whether one requires 95% or 99% clonal arrest.
source: we find that, to produce nevi of even 200 cells requires 4–5 independent events (stages), depending on whether one requires 95% or 99% clonal arrest; to reach 500 cells requires 6–7 events.
evidence: Results from multi-step simulations shown in Figure 4I

claim: To reach 500 cells requires 6–7 independent events.
source: to reach 500 cells requires 6–7 events.
evidence: Results from multi-step simulations shown in Figure 4I

claim: Cell-autonomous counting of cell cycles (up to about 12) can occur in early, cleavage-stage embryos.
source: Cell-autonomous counting of cell cycles (up to about 12) can occur in early, cleavage-stage embryos (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009

claim: No mechanism has been described to enable growing (as opposed to merely cleaving) cells to track more than a small handful of divisions (or the equivalent amount of time).
source: but no mechanism has been described to enable growing (as opposed to merely cleaving) cells to track more than a small handful of divisions (or the equivalent amount of time).
evidence: Statement about the state of scientific knowledge

claim: Erosion of telomeres does not seem to occur to any significant degree in nevus melanocytes.
source: Erosion of telomeres can mark the passage of large amounts of time in some cells, but this does not seem to occur to any significant degree in nevus melanocytes (Michaloglou et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Michaloglou et al., 2005

claim: If growth arrest is driven by cell–cell communication, then clock-like behavior is easily achieved, without any sort of intrinsic cell memory.
source: In contrast, if growth arrest is not cell-autonomous, but driven by cell–cell communication, then clock-like behavior is easily achieved, without any sort of intrinsic cell memory
evidence: Theoretical argument based on feedback control principles

claim: Renewal control is a feedback process that normal tissues use to control size.
source: This mechanism describes a dynamically well-understood feedback process that normal tissues use to control size (Lander, 2011; Lander et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lander, 2011 and Lander et al., 2009

claim: Renewal control is often mediated by secreted TGF-β superfamily members such as myostatin, activin and GDF11.
source: Termed 'renewal control' (Buzi et al., 2015), because differentiated cells control the probability that progenitor cells self-renew, the process is often mediated by secreted TGF-β superfamily members such as myostatin, activin and GDF11 (Gokoffski et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Renewal control produces highly robust final population sizes that are independent of parameters such as cell cycle speed or the starting numbers of cells.
source: Because it implements the engineering principle of 'integral negative feedback', renewal control produces highly robust final population sizes that are independent of parameters such as cell cycle speed or the starting numbers of cells (Buzi et al., 2015; Lander, 2011; Lander et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations describing the properties of renewal control

claim: When growth arrest due to renewal control is simulated as a probabilistic process, the observed size distributions of clones are very close to log-normal.
source: When growth arrest due to renewal control is simulated as a probabilistic process (Figure 5B), the observed size distributions of clones are very close to log-normal.
evidence: Results from simulations shown in Figure 5B

claim: Renewal control effectively enforces cell cooperation, so that once a small fraction of a clone has arrested, the entire clone stops soon thereafter.
source: This is because renewal control effectively enforces cell cooperation, so that once a small fraction of a clone has arrested, the entire clone stops soon thereafter.
evidence: Explanation of mechanism underlying simulation results

claim: Similar log-normal distributions are obtained whether nevi are modeled as progressing reversibly or irreversibly through more than one proliferative stage, or using agent-based simulations with diffusible molecules.
source: Similar distributions are obtained whether we model nevi as progressing reversibly or irreversibly through more than one proliferative stage, or use agent-based simulations in which renewal is controlled by the concentration of a secreted molecule that accumulates according to the laws of diffusion and local uptake (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Results from multiple simulation approaches shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: Nevus melanocytes express multiple genes encoding ligands with known or suspected growth inhibitory activities, together with the receptors for those ligands.
source: it is interesting that those cells that we identify as nevus melanocytes (Figure 2) express multiple genes encoding ligands with known or suspected growth inhibitory activities, together with the receptors for those ligands. These include TGFβ superfamily members Gdf11, Gdf15, Tgfb1, Tgfb2, and Tgfb3, as well as other genes associated with growth inhibition, such as Angptl2, Angptl4, Il6, Sema3a, Sema3b, and Sema3f (Attisano and Wrana, 1996; Neufeld et al., 2016; Santulli, 2014).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data and citations about gene functions

claim: Any feedback mechanism based on secreted, diffusible factors should induce spatial correlations among clones.
source: we reasoned that any feedback mechanism based on secreted, diffusible factors should induce spatial correlations among clones.
evidence: Theoretical prediction based on diffusion principles

claim: When clones (or subclones) get close enough to each other, they should inhibit each other's growth, leading to a smaller final size.
source: In particular, when clones (or subclones) get close enough to each other, they should inhibit each other's growth, leading to a smaller final size.
evidence: Theoretical prediction from feedback model

claim: The distance over which spatial effects could occur should reflect the spatial decay length of diffusible molecules in the skin, which is thought to be on the order of no more than a few hundred microns.
source: The distance over which such effects could occur should reflect the spatial decay length of diffusible molecules in the skin, which is thought to be on the order of no more than a few hundred microns (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015

claim: The median spacing between nests at postnatal day 21 was approximately 79 microns.
source: as the median spacing between nests at postnatal day 21 was approximately 79 microns.
evidence: Measurement from experimental data

claim: Within annuli extending 45 µm away from the perimeters of target nests, there were fewer examples of large neighbors (radius >30 µm) around large nests than around small ones.
source: As shown in Figure 5E–F, within annuli extending 45 µm away from the perimeters of target nests, we saw fewer examples of large neighbors (radius >30 µm) around large nests (panel E) than around small ones (panel F).
evidence: Spatial analysis results shown in Figure 5E-F

claim: The observed data extended outside of the envelopes of permuted data only for median neighbor sizes > 30 µm, with the data for small target nevi extending well above the relevant envelope and the data for large target nevi lying at to the bottom of the envelope.
source: Moreover, the observed data extended outside of the envelopes only for median neighbor sizes > 30 µm, with the data for small target nevi extending well above the relevant envelope and the data for large target nevi lying at to the bottom of the envelope (Figure 5E–F, arrows).
evidence: Statistical analysis results shown in Figure 5E-F

claim: Proximity is associated with a small, but significant decrease in nest size, supporting the view that nests inhibit each other's growth.
source: These results argue that proximity is associated with a small, but significant decrease in nest size, supporting the view that nests inhibit each other's growth.
evidence: Conclusion from spatial correlation analysis

claim: When annulus sizes of 150 µm were used, differences in the sizes of neighbors of small and large nests were not seen, consistent with the view that whatever is promoting coordination among nests has a spatial range of <150 µm.
source: Interestingly, when we repeated the same analysis using annulus sizes of 150 µm, differences in the sizes of neighbors of small and large nests were not seen, consistent with the view that whatever is promoting coordination among nests has a spatial range of <150 µm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Spatial analysis results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Studies in man, mouse and fish establish that most melanocytic nevi form by mutational activation of BRAF, which triggers proliferation followed by growth arrest.
source: Studies in man, mouse and fish establish that most melanocytic nevi form by mutational activation of BRAF, which triggers proliferation followed by growth arrest (Damsky and Bosenberg, 2017; Dankort et al., 2009; Dhomen et al., 2009; Kaufman et al., 2016; Michaloglou et al., 2005; Patton et al., 2005; Shain and Bastian, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies in different species

claim: Across a wide variety of gene expression signatures, especially those developed to distinguish senescence from other growth-arrested cell states, we failed to find any evidence in support of the OIS hypothesis.
source: Across a wide variety of gene expression signatures, especially those developed to distinguish senescence from other growth-arrested cell states, we failed to find any evidence in support of the OIS hypothesis.
evidence: Summary of gene expression signature analysis results

claim: By gene expression criteria, nevus melanocytes were less senescent than many other normal skin cells, including non-nevus melanocytes.
source: By gene expression criteria, nevus melanocytes were less senescent than many other normal skin cells, including non-nevus melanocytes (Figure 3, and its supplements).
evidence: Summary of gene expression signature analysis results shown in figures

claim: These results support earlier work that also questioned, based on immunohistochemical staining of human nevi for markers including lysosomal β-galactosidase, Ki67, p16INK4a (CDKN2A), γ-H2AX and p53, whether nevus melanocytes should be considered senescent.
source: These results support earlier work that also questioned, based on immunohistochemical staining of human nevi for markers including lysosomal β-galactosidase, Ki67, p16INK4a (CDKN2A), γ-H2AX and p53, whether nevus melanocytes should be considered senescent (Tran et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tran et al., 2012

claim: Cdkn2A is highly expressed in nevus cells and is the only 'classical' senescence marker that clearly distinguishes nevus melanocytes from other melanocytes.
source: In agreement with other studies, we do find that Cdkn2A is highly expressed in nevus cells; it is in fact the only 'classical' senescence marker that clearly distinguishes nevus melanocytes from other melanocytes (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Cdkn2A is neither necessary nor sufficient for oncogene-mediated melanocyte growth arrest.
source: Yet, as others have shown, Cdkn2A is neither necessary nor sufficient for oncogene-mediated melanocyte growth arrest (Haferkamp et al., 2009; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haferkamp et al., 2009 and Zeng et al., 2018

claim: To the extent that nevus melanocytes do execute even part of a common senescence program, there is little to support the view that this why they stop proliferating.
source: Thus, to the extent that nevus melanocytes do execute even part of a common senescence program, there is little to support the view that this why they stop proliferating.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from gene expression and functional data

claim: The in vivo data do not support the hypothesis that IGFBP7 plays a necessary role in BRAF-V600E-induced melanocyte senescence.
source: Our in vivo data do not support any of these hypotheses. For example, we observed that the vast majority of Igfbp7 transcripts are produced by fibroblasts and endothelial cells and that, among melanocytes, nevus melanocytes express lower levels of Igfbp7 than non-nevus melanocytes.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data

claim: Mia transcripts were not detected in nevus melanocytes, although it was expressed at detectable levels in non-nevus melanocytes and various other skin cells.
source: We did not detect any Mia transcripts in nevus melanocytes, although it was expressed at detectable levels in non-nevus melanocytes and various other skin cells.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data

claim: Of Il1 family members, only Il1a transcripts were detected in nevus melanocytes and they were at levels lower than in many other skin cell types.
source: Likewise, of Il1 family members, only Il1a transcripts were detected in nevus melanocytes and they were at levels lower than in many other skin cell types.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data

claim: Il6 was only weakly expressed in nevus melanocytes, especially when compared with other cells.
source: Il6 was also only weakly expressed in nevus melanocytes, especially when compared with other cells.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data

claim: Transcripts for type one interferons were not detected in any melanocytic cells, and Cxcl15 transcripts were not detected in any skin cells at all.
source: Transcripts for type one interferons were not detected in any melanocytic cells, and Cxcl15 transcripts were not detected in any skin cells at all.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data

claim: The authors strongly favor the renewal-feedback model (model C) over OIS models.
source: But given these results, and the evidence that nevus melanocytes are not senescent, we strongly favor the renewal-feedback model (model C).
evidence: Conclusion based on the totality of evidence presented

claim: Nevi may exhibit a low level of mitoses.
source: For example, it is known that nevi may exhibit a low level of mitoses (Glatz et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Glatz et al., 2010

claim: Nevi can grow in response to stimuli such as UV light or immunosuppression.
source: that they can grow in response to stimuli such as UV light (Rudolph et al., 1998) or immunosuppression (Shain and Bastian, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rudolph et al., 1998 and Shain and Bastian, 2016

claim: Nevi can re-grow after incomplete surgical resection—stopping again when they reach a typical nevus size.
source: and, perhaps most tellingly, they can re-grow after incomplete surgical resection—stopping again when they reach a typical nevus size (Vilain et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vilain et al., 2016

claim: The re-growth of nevi after incomplete surgical resection is inherently problematic for any non-feedback model, but is precisely what renewal feedback predicts.
source: The latter result is inherently problematic for any non-feedback model, but is precisely what renewal feedback predicts (Lander, 2011; Lander et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference based on theoretical predictions of feedback models

claim: During anagen phase of the hair cycle, melanocyte stem cells produce progeny that migrate out of the hair follicle bulge as they differentiate, leaving functional stem cells behind for future cycles.
source: For instance, during anagen phase of the hair cycle, melanocyte stem cells produce progeny that migrate out of the hair follicle bulge as they differentiate, leaving functional stem cells behind for future cycles.
evidence: Statement of established biological knowledge

claim: Experimental and pathological circumstances that allow small numbers of melanocytes to differentiate within the bulge cause differentiation and loss of the entire stem cell pool (with concomitant hair graying).
source: A variety of experimental and pathological circumstances that allow small numbers of melanocytes to differentiate within the bulge cause differentiation and loss of the entire stem cell pool (with concomitant hair graying [Nishimura et al., 2005]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nishimura et al., 2005

claim: The behavior where differentiated cells drive the differentiation of their progenitors is exactly the sort of behavior that drives feedback models of renewal.
source: This sort of behavior—where differentiated cells drive the differentiation of their progenitors—is exactly the sort of behavior that drives feedback models of renewal (Buzi et al., 2015; Lander, 2011; Lander et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference connecting observed biological behavior to theoretical models

claim: Nevi are but one of many types of benign, clonal, proliferative lesions that arise due to the activation of oncogenes, but rarely if ever progress to malignancy.
source: Nevi are but one of many types of benign, clonal, proliferative lesions that arise due to the activation of oncogenes, but rarely if ever progress to malignancy (Adashek et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adashek et al., 2020

claim: The existence of benign oncogene-driven lesions suggests that homeostatic mechanisms persist and function at many stages along the road to cancer.
source: Notwithstanding the disruptive influence that oncogenes can have on cell physiology, the existence of such lesions suggest that homeostatic mechanisms persist and function at many stages along the road to cancer.
evidence: Inference from the observation of benign oncogene-driven lesions

claim: New avenues for cancer prevention and treatment are likely to follow from the detailed elucidation of homeostatic mechanisms.
source: New avenues for cancer prevention and treatment are likely to follow from the detailed elucidation of such mechanisms.
evidence: Speculative statement about future research directions

claim: The average nevus has about 500–1000 cells, but given possible errors in the estimate, a range of values between 100 and 3000 is considered.
source: As described below (see Materials and methods), we estimate that the average nevus has about 500–1000 cells, but given possible errors in the estimate, we consider here a range of values between 100 and 3000 (gray-shaded area in Figure 4I).
evidence: Estimation based on measurements described in Materials and methods

claim: Using 8 µm sections of back skin from Albino BrafV600E mice, an average cell diameter of 5.68 µm was measured for melanocytes within the nests of nevi.
source: Using 8 µm sections of back skin from Albino BrafV600E mice, we used fluorescence microscopy to measure the sizes of 194 Pmel-stained melanocytes within the nests of nevi, obtaining an average cell diameter of 5.68 µm
evidence: Measurement from experimental data

claim: Approximately 14.4 cells per 104 µm3 of nest were counted in albino BrafV600E mice.
source: and counted approximately 14.4 cells per 104 µm3 of nest.
evidence: Measurement from experimental data

claim: In pigmented animals, an average nest cross sectional area of 1385 µm2, an average nest volume of 38792 µm3, and an average number of nests per nevi of approximately 12 were measured, yielding an estimate of 672 cells/nevus.
source: In pigmented animals, we measured by MPM an average nest cross sectional area of 1385 µm2, an average nest volume of 38792 µm3, and an average number of nests per nevi of approximately 12, yielding an estimate of 672 cells/nevus.
evidence: Measurements from experimental data
